title: Roger Pryor Dodge and early jazz criticism
summary: The chapter 'Consider the Critics', Charles Edward Smith's early writing, and Dodge's earlier articles.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Do you know anything about Roger Pryor Dodge?
Yeah, I knew him quite well.

I tell you, I read that chapter, Consider the Critics. This is one of the first things I read when I picked up the book, because at that time, three, four years ago, I was very interested in how jazz, early jazz, or New Orleans jazz, got to be known nationally. And I had always thought that certain New Orleans musicians brought jazz to Chicago and then to New York, and it was popularized through people like Louie, etc. But then I began to realize that the New Orleans tradition was brought to the public attention through a select group of people, not through popular writers. It was brought through record collectors and certain critics who had started writing about it. And then I became interested in the subject of how jazz was acculturated, I guess you could use that word, through record collectors and critics to an almost specialized audience. That is not to the national popular attention, but to a specialized audience of jazz people that were jazz enthusiasts. That became almost a specialized activity. Well, this chapter, Consider the Critics, traced things that had been said about jazz and the prejudices that had always been carried from one writing to another. And then when Charles Edward Smith wrote an article in the symposium in 1930, there seemed to be somewhat of a breakthrough. And I guess he seems to put Charles Edward Smith in the role of seeing jazz as a musical form and not as something that needed to be extended into a musical form by classical musicians or people that really know about music.

So, yeah, Dodd, I wrote a very early article too, if I remember rightly. I don't know if it mentions it in there or anything. Back in the twenties, he'd written, I have in mind maybe 1927, as early as that. About jazz.
Is that right? No. It's funny because.
I don't know where we could find out about that or where it's mentioned.
There are bibliographies. We can look it up.
It says here in the introduction, he wrote the first serious study of jazz published in this country, this symposium, 1930. And then the first popular article on it in Esquire in 1934.
Dodd had written something earlier than that, I'm quite sure.
So, anyway, he was a very, very nice guy, I always thought.
